submission.natural_language_explanation: Bimodal single-anchor pointer: at each token the head either parks on a sink (the passage's first token or a period) and writes ~0, or locks (attention ~1.0) onto one earlier-or-current anchor token and copies it onward to the following tokens. It locks strongly (1.1-2.0 of max) when the anchor is a digit numeral (years like 1932, numbers like 273, 42, 841) or a concrete or technical noun/subword (cigarette, smoke, virus, mitochondria, engine, non-Latin script pieces); it locks weakly (0.6-1.1) on everyday concrete nouns and activity words (dog, apple, milk, dinner, play), so about half of plain prose is active-weak; it stays at 0 across clauses made only of pronouns, person nouns (man, king, doctor, friend), abstract nouns (plan, idea, time, journey, epistemology) and spelled-out numbers (seven, nine).

rival_explanations: Rarity reading: strength tracks the unigram rarity of whatever token the head locks onto, so rare abstract words (epistemology, ontology) should anchor strongly and common person nouns should not matter, whereas the hypothesis predicts abstract rare words stay near the sink and only numerals and concrete/technical nouns anchor strongly.

Syntactic-juncture reading: the head fires on function words and punctuation (and, of, near, =, commas) that follow any content word, regardless of that word's class, so 'The man was near the old wall' and 'They discussed the plan for an hour' should fire as much as their concrete-noun twins.
